Mr. Speaker,
may I be allowed to put the facts before the House? The committee on privileges and elections, of which I have the honour to be the chairman, has been called together on four different occasions, but we were unable to proceed for lack of a quorum. Without a quorum the committee could not sit and consequently could not report to the House. At the instance of some members of the committee I moved in the House to have the quorum reduced to eight or nine members, and objection was taken by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) on the ground that as this was a very important committee the quorum should not be reduced. I must admit that I had not up to that time given much thought to the matter, but it struck me that probably it might be just as well not to reduce the quorum. maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO ON MILK AND CREAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the House a matter of vital importance to our section of the country and to those border counties in the province of Quebec which ship milk and cream to the United States.
1642	COMMONS
Canadian Minister at Washington
A headline in a local newspaper says: "Milk and cream embargo hits eastern townships farmers." I desire to ask the Minister of Agriculture a question, but before doing so I would like to be permitted to explain that the market for the cream produced in the district surrounding Sherbrooke and to the south of that city is in Boston and the New England states; cream from this section has not been shipped to the city of Montreal. Therefore I think the government should immediately take this question up with Washington through our new minister and see to it that the embargo is lifted at once. This is the season of the year when the milk supply is increasing, and the matter is of vital importance. I ask the Minister of Agriculture if anything is being done in this connection.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: UNITED STATES EMBARGO ON MILK AND CREAM
speechtext: I would say to my hon. friend that about noon yesterday we received official information through the Department of External Affairs, and they in turn through Hon. Mr. Massey at Washington, that this embargo had been placed on Canadian milk and cream due to an outbreak of typhoid in Montreal, thought to be caused by an infected milk supply. Immediately the officers of my department got in touch with the Department of Health and with the medical health officer of the city of Montreal, to see exactly what was the situation and what could be done in order to expedite the discovery of the source of contagion. We had a telephone message from the medical health officer of Montreal this morning, but the only information we were able to elicit was that the contagion was pretty general and that the source had not yet been discovered, either in the city through the medium of any dairy or in the country at the source of supply. Mr. Stephens of the National Dairy Council was in communication with the Secretary of Agriculture, Mr. Jar-dine, at Washington, in the hope of raising the embargo as it would affect those localities which have not shipped any cream or milk to Montreal for the past six months. Until twelve o'clock to-day, however, no word had been received with respect to that matter, and that is where the matter stands at present. Everything is being done to locate the source of contagion, but until the source is located and the contagion removed I am afraid the general embargo cannot be lifted, although it may be taken off as against those localities which are not now and have not for the past six months shipped milk to Montreal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by agreement between the different parties in the House it was arranged that this afternoon a statement should be made with regard to the proceedings of the recent Imperial conference, and that following the statement hon. members should be free to discuss the conference proceedings before Your Honour leaves the chair. Subsequently in committee on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs any matters of detail on which hon. members may wish to have further information can be elaborated.
It may perhaps answer in advance questions that will arise in the minds of some hon. gentlemen opposite, and help to remove doubts as to the position of the present administration in ithe matter of its representation at the recent conference, if I mention to the House that the first- intimation the former Liberal government had of the intention to hold an Imperial conference in 1926 was last year in the month of January. At that time a communication was received from the British government asking if it was probable that Canada would be able to be represented at a confertence in the month of June, or later in the year. A reply was sent to that communication indicating that political conditions were more or less uncertain in Canada, and that it was doubtful whether anyone would be in a position to leave to attend an - Imperial conference in June. It was suggested that the conference might better be postponed for another year, but if not for a year at least till the fall. As hon. members know, when June came political conditions were very unsettled. During the concluding months of last year's session members of the administration had very little time to give to the problems that were to come up at the conference. Indeed the intention was, had the government remained in office, to take advantage of the period of recess that would follow the session carefully to prepare with respect to the various subjects on the agenda. However, the Liberal administration resigned at the end of June, and the Conservative administration then took office. That administration continued in office until on in September; I doubt if during that period the hon. members of that administration had any time to give to Imperial conference matters. When we resumed office the date set for the conference was upon us.
I mention this simply to bring out the circumstance that when my hon. colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and I left to attend the Imperial conference in September we had had no opportunity whatever of study-

Imperial Conjerence-Mr. Mackenzie King
ing the agenda, and were really scarcely aware of the subjects that were to come up for discussion. There is one point, however, that I would like to make quite clear, and it is this, the moment the government came into office it decided that Canada would be represented at the conference, regardless of how inconvenient that might be to those members of the administration who might represent the Dominion. Upon resuming office in September the first communication I addressed was to the Prime Minister of Great Britain to say that the Minister of Justice and myself would represent Canada at the Imperial conference and that we hoped to be able to be present on the opening day of its proceedings.
The conference opened on October 19 and continued its sittings until November 23. During that time there were twenty-three plenary sessions of the conference. May I make clear at the outset that the conference in character was what by name it is described as having been; namely a conference. I't was a conference of the prime ministers together with other ministers of the dominions and of the British government discussing matters of mutual interest and common concern, but in no sense was it a cabinet council. At a preceding conference great care was taken by my colleagues and myself to make it clear that we had no authority from the parliament of Canada to become members of an Imperial council seeking to lay down policies with regard to imperial affairs; that we were there as representatives of the Dominion of Canada to confer with representatives of other governments of the empire, to reach such conclusions as it might be possible to reach and then to report them to our respective parliaments, but that we had no authority whatever to bind in any particular in advance the parliament of our country. That position was restated at the opening of the recent conference, and I therefore hope that from the outset it will be clear to hon. members that in no particular has this parliament or this country been bound by any conclusions that were reached by members of the conference that met last fall.
An effort was made with respect to the different questions on the agenda to reach a common agreement, and common agreement was arrived at with respect to practically all the matters which appeared on the agenda. That common agreement finds expression in the report of the conference, and in the course of my remarks this afternoon I shall assume that hon. members not only have received copies of this report but that if they are at
all interested in the proceedings of the conference they will have perused the report. There has been laid on the table not only a printed copy of the proceedings of the conference but a supplementary volume in the nature of appendices and a larger summary of the proceedings. These two documents give the main outline of the proceedings of the conference.
Perhaps I should mention to the House the method and order of procedure adopted in conference. The representatives of the several dominions and of the British government met around the council table at No. 10 Downing street. The proceedings opened by a short address delivered by the Prime Minister of Great Britain. Mr. Baldwin reviewed the proceedings of preceding conferences and also gave an outline of recent developments on matters of inter-imperial interest. The address of the Prime Minister of Great Britain was followed by addresses by the prime ministers of the other dominions. They will be found in full in the printed report of the appendices to which I have just referred.
Following the introductory addresses the question of trade within the empire was next dealt with at a plenary conference. Addresses were delivered by the President of the Board of Trade and by the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs outlining the point of view of the British government with respect to inter-imperial trade and questions relating thereto. This general review was followed by similar reviews by representatives of the different dominions.
The next subject to be considered was that of foreign affairs; perhaps I should not say foreign affairs-I should make the statement broader and say inter-imperial as well as foreign relations. The Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs delivered an address outlining at considerable length Britain's foreign relations in all of the countries of the world, basing his statements upon the latest information gathered from the various embassies and legations of Great Britain in different parts of the globe, and also upon the accumulation of data which has its existence in the Foreign Office. That statement was necessarily highly confidential and it could not be given to the public generally. It was followed by statements on the part of the prime ministers of the different dominions with respect to those external relations of their countries which they felt might be of special interest to those assembled.
It was thought that the constitutional questions were so far-reaching and also appeared in such numbers on the agenda that it would

Imperial Conference-Mr. Mackenzie King
not be advisable to have those questions discussed at a full conference, but that better progress could be made if the constitutional issues were referred to a committee of the conference where there would be greater freedom of discussion than at a large meeting at which shorthand notes were taken of all the proceedings. Accordingly a committee, of which the Right Hon. the Earl of Balfour was chairman, was appointed to deal with the question of constitutional relations as they affected both relations within the empire and the relations of the dominions and Great Britain with foreign countries. When that committee met it was found advisable to appoint from its number a sub-committee to deal with one special phase, namely that which relates to the negotiation, signing and ratification of treaties and matters pertaining to conferences at which different parts of the empire may be represented. My colleague the Minister of Justice was named chairman of that committee. I shall come back a little later on to the conclusions of these various committees. I am at the moment merely seeking to give a review which will indicate the scope of the work of the conference as a whole.
Next in interest to foreign affairs and interimperial relations as a subject of general discussion at the conference was the question of defence. This was dealt with in the first instance by the Prime Minister of Great Britain, then by the senior officer of the chiefs of staff sub-committee. Admiral of the Fleet, Earl Beatty, in a survey of the general strategic situation. Meetings also took place at the Admiralty, the War Office, and the Air Ministry, in which the situation from the standpoint of His Majesty's government in Great Britain was presented in greater detail. These meetings and addresses of the Minister for Gar, First Lord of the Admiralty and the Minister for Air were followed by addresses^ on the part of representatives of the Dominions with respect to the services-army, navy, and air-of the respective dominions. Matters which were thought to be of special interest to the conference as a whole were brought to its attention in that manner.
In addition to the general review which took place at the full conference, and the detailed discussions at the admirality, at the A\ar Office, and at the Air Ministry, at which experts gave an account in a more detailed way of some of the problems of defence that from the British point of view were considered by the British government as important enough to bring before the conference as a whole, there were demonstrations of the various arms of the service in operation at

different centres illustrative of the developments of modern warfare-a naval review off Portland, an army mechanical display at Camberley, and air demonstrations at Croydon and Cardington.
In addition to these main subjects of interest, trade, foreign affairs, inter-imperial relations, and defence, a number of economic questions were brought up for consideration. Hon. members may recall that in 1923 there were two conferences which carried on their proceedings simultaneously; there rvas the Imperial conference so-called, and the Imperial economic conference. At the Economic conference, questions relating to economic matters were discussed. On this occasion there was but one conference, with the result that so far as economic questions were concerned, they for the most part came to be dealt with bj' permanent officials of the different governments accompanying the delegations or resident in London. They took up questions that in part had been, prior to the meeting of the conference, the subject of communication between the different governments. Economic matters that were thought to be of sufficient importance to bring before the conference as a whole were brought before it in its concluding days. After the various committees had met, there was placed before the body as a whole the various conclusions to which the different committees had come.
I should like to bring out this fact, if I may, that throughout the conference, with respect to the different matters placed before the conference, its members seemed to desire not to discover points of difference, but rather to arrive at as many points of agreement as might be possible. May I say with reference to the British ministers whom we met, that I failed to discover from the beginning to the close of the conference the slightest evidence of any desire to treat the matters before the conference from a party point of view. Nothing could have been fairer, nothing oould have been more patriotic in the true sense of the word, than the manner in which, from beginning to close, the British government dealt with the representatives of the other governments present at the conference. I stress that at the moment because I hope that in our own parliament these matters of inter-imperial interests and concern may be viewed from a higher level than that of questions of party politics giving rise to party controversy. I shall sincerely endeavour in presenting this subject this afternoon to present it from what I may say expresses the Canadian point of view rather than from the point of view of the representative of a political party in this House.

Imperial Conference-Mr. Mackenzie King
Coming to the proceedings of the conference, I will take up first those which are to us, of less immediate concern and reserve for the 'concluding part of my remarks the subjects in which I think the House is more especially interested, at least at the present time.
The economic questions might, I think, be omitted from discussion at the present moment. more particularly as all that I would be in a position to say about them will be found fully covered in the report which the House has before it.
I will just enumerate the subjects that are dealt with in the report: overseas settlement, workmen's compensation, research, forestry, exhibition within the empire of empire films, industrial standardization, Imperial shipping committee and Imperial economic committee, maritime conventions, oil pollution of navigable waters, statistical questions, and taxation questions. So far as these various questions are concerned, I do not think there is anything of a controversial character in the report. The effort of those who were assembled at the conference was with respect to many of these matters to find more effective means of gathering statistical data and of coordinating efforts between different parts of the empire.
Perhaps I might say one word on the subject of overseas settlement, as being of more interest to the House than any of the other topics. One thing that was apparent in the discussion of migration was that in all parts of the world the unsettled conditions had very materially changed the situation in the matter of emigrants. In presenting the Canadian point of view of overseas settlement, attention was drawn to the fact that immigration to Canada through government assistance is not as easy a matter as it was some years ago. There are not available at the present time lands which can be given away as homesteads, and in addition, the cost of transportation by ocean has increased very materially. The social laws of England, providing funds for the unemployed, have made it from the point of view of some persons less desirable to emigrate than formerly. With respect to assistance. I think it is true that the present administration has gone further than any previous administration in assisting migration from Great Britain to this country. Under the British Empire three-thousand family settlement scheme, this government has entered into a generous arrangement with the British government in regard to bringing settlers here. One step that was taken during the conference was to provide for the inspection of immigrants by medical services
established in Great Britain, so that emigrants could leave the shores of Great Britain with the certainty of being admitted here, at least, so far as the test of physical fitness is concerned, and not have to run the risk which has been a deterrent in many cases in the past of being obliged to return after having crossed the ocean. The government's policy has been to assist agricultural labourers, domestic servants and juvenile immigrants, but to confine its assistance in the matter of assisted passages to those classes. The report upon the work being done in Canada made by the British officials who visited this country last year was one of a highly commendatory character.
On the subject of communication, there were taken up methods of improving the steamship services as between different parts of the empire. The question of the Pacific cable came up incidentally, and an agreement was reached between the different governments as to the basis upon which future reserve funds should be expended. Other points that have been in dispute between different parts of the empire were satisfactorily settled and an agreement was arrived at under which a bill was to be introduced in the British parliament. This has since been done.
On imperial air communications, I Should perhaps mention that the discussion helped to make apparent that we are on the eve of a vast development in long distance flights. Possibly no part of the conference was more impressive than that which related to the development of aerial navigation and air services, not only as factors in times of war but as agencies in the pro-motion of peace and progress. Fortunately, so far as Canada is concerned, it was possible to make a statement of the part played by our air services, which was of the highest character. During the period of the war, though this country had no aerial service, it did contribute 10,009 men to the air force, and since the war there has been a very great development, largely on the civil aviation side. With respect to surveys, the patrolling of forests, of coast areas and in other directions, a marked advance has been made by the Canadian service.
The British government intimated that they were anxious to experiment in airship flights, and asked the dominions if they would cooperate toward that end. It appeared to my colleague and myself that the citizens of Canada would wish to have this country cooperate closely with Great Britain in an experimental air service between the British Isles and the Dominion, and we undertook- it was the only undertaking we gave without

I come now to what, from the point of view of this dominion, I assume to be the most important of all the matters discussed at the conference, namely, constitutional issues and questions relating thereto. First of all may I explain how these questions came to play the important part which they did in the conference proceedings? I mentioned the other day that Canada did not put forward concretely any particular matters to be taken up at the conference. I should not like that statement to be construed as meaning that Canada has played no part with respect to many of the questions that were raised. As a matter of fact the position which this country has taken all along of being a selfgoverning dominion with full right to control its own domestic affairs, both internal and external, necessarily brought to the fore many important questions which seemed to suggest a possible conflict with that point of view. Some of these questions we in Canada have long since worked out satisfactorily, but they are assuming an importance in other parts of the empire similar to that which they assumed here many years ago. ing impression one receives from a conference such as the Imperial conference is the vast difference that exists between the different dominions of the British Empire. To refer to the dominions as a class, as though they were all of a type, is I think a mistake. There is need for the recognition of the individuality within the empire of each separate dominion. There are differences of historical background, of racial composition, of economic development and of political evolution, all of which go far to make the differences between the dominions themselves vastly greater in many particulars, than any differences 'between	this Dominion
and Great Britain. It is largely for that reason that some of the questions which created a good deal of discussion at the conference were brought forward. Questions that we, as I have said, have regarded as settled for many years past, have come to assume an importance in South Africa and in the Irish Free State which they have not assumed here for many years, and naturally those countries were interested in having all such questions determined.
Broadly speaking, the first duty and effort of the committee that dealt with the constitutional questions was to formulate a statement which would clearly define the position that has been attained by the selfgoverning dominions in their relation to Great Britain. That position is set forth in the report as one of equality of status, permitting of free cooperation between the different parts of the empire. It is natural that the constitutional questions should assume a considerable magnitude when we recall the fact that the transition from a relationship within the empire of imperial control and colonial subordination to one of equality of status, with free cooperation between the different parts, is the greatest political transition that possibly the world has witnessed, the most momentous, and the most unprecedented political development of modern times. It was inevitable that this transformation, which has gone on with special rapidity since the war should create new problems that would have to be faced, should make it necessary from time to time to take stock, to consider ways and means of making forms correspond to facts, and of adjusting relations with foreign countries to the new conditions. So far as the dominions were concerned, in their relation to Britain, they started out in a position of colonial subordination. It was recognized that there was an

Imperial control over the dominions. In the course of years, however, by here a little being gained and there a little, in the political evolution that has occurred, a change ha?, come about; and whatever we may say when we come to refining from technical and legal points of view, we no longer think of the dominions as being in a position of colonial subordination nor of the British government as in a position of Imperial control in relation to other parts of the empire.
To solve the constitutional question it was necessary to find some common ground and agreement on the part of all sections of the empire regarding the new status which has been attained. How that status has been attained and to whom the credit is due is another question that can be discussed by itself. Certain it is, however, that to no one group or cause is the change to be attributed: it is part of the evolution of the last half century, an evolution that was tremendously accentuated by the war. The change that has come about is one that can be described as a change from a position of Imperial control and colonial subordination to one, as I have already said, of equality of status and free cooperation as between the dominions and Great Britain. That being set out as the basis of a common agreement, it became necessary to consider in relation thereto many forms which, if not entirely, at any rate to some extent, have become obsolete and which appear to be in conflict with the altered situation. That brought up various constitutional questions which were the subject of considerable discussion. Once having stated clearly that the position attained to-day was one of equality of status, it then became necessary to examine, in the light of that statement, existing legal, judicial or administrative forms which seemed to be in conflict therewith, and to see how far these obsolete forms were a vital consideration. That was how the committee came to give so much time to the consideration of some of the matters to which I shall now refer.
May I be allowed to quote to the House the statement Which was agreed upon as setting forth the present position) of the dominions, on the one hand, and of Great Britain on the other, in their relation to each other. And here let me stress this point: this statement relates not to the strictly legal position but to the constitutional status which has been reached. In a speech recently delivered in Edinburgh Lord Balfour declared that law had always followed a little behind1 constitutional practice and development; and that very sound opinion, I think, may well be kept

I will read the paragraphs of the report which bring out the significant passage:
The committee are of opinion that nothing would be gained by attempting to lay down a constitution for the British Empire. Its widely scattered parts have very different characteristics, very different histories, and are at very different stages of evolution; while, considered as a whole, it defies classification and bears no real resemblance to any other political organization which now exists or has ever yet been tried.
There is, however, one most important element in it which, from a strictly constitutional point of view, has now, as regards all vital matters, reached its full development-we refer to the group of self-governing communities composed of Great Britain and the dominions. Their position and mutual relation may be readily defined. They are autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
The significant points in that statement are, first, the emphasis it places upon the complete autonomy of the dominions in the matter of their own domestic and external affairs, and secondly, the allegiance to a common sovereign. These two are stressed as being points of agreement among the various parts of the empire as represented at the conference.
Let us now consider this general statement, taking up in turn existing forms or laws that seem in conflict with it. As a first, not in order of consideration but as illustrating the evolution that has taken place, let me begin with the king's title. The conference decided to change the title of His * Majesty the king. That change grew out of the altered position of the Irish Free State, which is one of the self-governing autonomous dominions. The title of His Majesty heretofore has always been "of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland," et cetera, "King". It was pointed out by representatives of the Irish Free State that inasmuch as that state was a self-governing dominion, and an agreement having been reached at the time of its establishment that it should be placed in the same category as the other dominions, it should no longer be linked up with the United Kingdom in. the description of the king's title. By agreement, therefore, between the British government and the Irish Free State it was proposed that the title should read: of Great Britain, Ireland and the British Dominions beyond the Seas, King," et cetera, it being understood that the title

The next subject to be mentioned in this connection relates to the position of the governor general. I have already stated that the change from a position of colonial subordination to one of equality of status as regards the dominions has been a matter of political evolution. When governors general were first appointed to this country-just as governors, are appointed to-day to the colonies- there was an acknowledged position of colonial subordination in the relation of the Dominion to the mother country. That, however, has long since passed away, and the position of Governor General has come to be understood as that Of the representative of His Majesty the King. Speaking in a previous debate the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) said that the position of Governor General had in no particular been changed, that it was set forth in the British North America Act and remained as stated there.
1 agree with my hon. friend as to that; the position has not been changed but what has been changed is this:	It is now perfectly
clear that the Governor General is advised by the ministry of the Dominion to which he comes, and is no longer free to accept advice from His Majesty's government or from any department of that government with reference to the affairs of the Dominion of which he is Governor General.

The vital question of Mr. King's action in advising Lord Byng to consult Mr. Amery appears to me to have been seriously misunderstood. No one could deny that Lord Byng was an Imperial officer subject to the royal instructions, conveyed through the Secretary of State. The point at issue was-what did these instructions enjoin in the case where a prime minister asked for a dissolution, and presented for approval an order in council for that purpose? Was it Lord Byng's duty to investigate the political situation for himself, and decide on his own responsibility what was best for Canada? Or could lie follow the British practice-recently signally illustrated by the immediate acceptance by His Majesty of Mr. Ramsay MacDonald's advice in 1924- and act on the advice of his ministers? The custom of the Australian states supported the use of a personal discretion, but no Canadian Governor General since federation had ever declined advice. Lord Byng was without political experience, and it appears to me that Mr. King acted with much common sense in advising him, before taking a decision which, as he rightly anticipated would have very far-reaching consequences, to ask the Secretary of State what the royal instructions really meant. 1 confess that, while I have always held that Lord Byng erred in his decision, it appears to me that much of the responsibility really rests with a system under which a Governor General is sent out without any clear instructions as to the place which he is to occupy in the structure of government. I pass to the next subject that came up, and that is the system of communication between the British government and our government. In the old days of colonial subordination all communications came from the

Imperial Conference-Mr. Mackenzie King
British government to the Canadian government through the Governor General. The practice began when the Governor General was avowedly the agent of the British government. During the war a new practice was adopted of direct communication between the prime minister of a dominion and the Prime Minister of Great Britain. There has been no definitely established practice since then, and in view of the declaration that the Governor General was representing His Majesty the King and was not the representative of the British government, it became important to consider whether the custom of always forwarding communications to a Dominion government through the Governor General should be continued or not. It was felt by the conference that there was no more reason, logically or constitutionally, why communications should be sent from the government of Great Britain to a Canadian minister or Prime Minister through His Excellency the Governor General, than why a communication from the Canadian government to the Prime Minister of England or the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs should be sent through His Majesty the King. It was decided that, having regard to the equality of status, the practice that should be adopted hereafter would be one of direct communication of government with government, thereby eliminating the possibility of a Governor General being drawn into controversy or discussion with respect to despatches that are immediately passing between governments. It will take a little while to have this new arrangement worked out, but it is being worked out at the present time.
The next subject was that of the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties, and the representation of the dominions along with the British government at conferences and gatherings at which the representation of all or a certain number might be expected. If my hon. friend will allow me, I think I can explain to him wherein this has a significance. So far as the question of disallowance is concerned, it is not a matter of any great concern to this parliament or to this country because it has not been exercised for fifty years, and we have no fears of its being exercised. But take the position of Ireland, and then you begin to see why this question was brought up at the Imperial conference, and why the interpretation which the British ministry has placed upon it is a wise one. The Irish Free State came into existence in 1921, and one of the clauses of the act bringing it into existence provided with respect to constitutional questions, that matters affecting the Irish Free State would be carried out in accordance with the practice and custom of Canada. That is what made it important to have an interpretation, so far as Canada was concerned, of the significance of disallowance.
Now may I draw this to the attention of the House? In the Irish Free State you have a body of members who have separated from those in the north of Ireland. They have withdrawn the representation which they formerly had in the British House of Commons, having now their own parliament dealing with their own affairs. If you grant that the power of disallowance lies in the hands of the British government, then, so far as the Irish Free State is concerned, the situation is this: that the men who within the last three or four years have been given the right of self-government are obliged to have all their legislation subject to disallowance by a government that politically may be hostile to them. Does not my hon. friend agree with me that I am entitled to- say that that is the kind of a situation which agitators delight in? All that is needed to create trouble in southern Ireland with respect to the power of disallowance is to point out that gentlemen sitting at Westminster, who politically are the sworn enemies of the right of self-government in the Irish Free State, have the right to disallow any act of the parliament of that state. The British government took the broad view that such a situation should not be allowed to develop in that way, and they have given in clear terms their own interpretation of what their course of action with respect to disallowance will be. The British government themselves have done this. They have said with relation to legislation passed by the parliament of the Irish Free State that they would not disallow such legislation except upon the advice of the ministers of the Free State parliament, not the ministers of the British parliament. Is not that the sort of thing that makes for unity and harmony within the empire? And the same thing is true in its application to South Africa. South Africa has grave racial problems. An agitator there can make capital of the fact that legislation passed by the South African parliament may be disallowed by the British parliament. But the minute that the British government come forward with a broad liberal principle and say we will so far as this power of disallowance is concerned exercise it in a constitutional way, namely, where there is a selfgoverning dominion we will recognize equality of status and we will have that power of disallowance exercised only on the advice of the ministry of the dominion concerned, there all possibility of agitation is at an end. That was the principle laid down with respect to disallowance. And so I might go on and say with regard to sucih matters as the right of appeal to the Privy Council that there again the position was clearly stated, that it was fertile dominion itself, possessing self-government to the fullest extent, to say whether or not it wished that right of appeal limited, cancelled or continued. In other words, what the British government, along with the other dominions sought to do wias to make it clear that when we speak of self-government- autonomy-in relation to domestic and external affairs, the words mean exactly what we say they do. I shall leave this part, because it gets into the realm of legal controversy, to my friend the Minister of Justice to deal with.

Lett us listen to the statements. Lord Parmoor, taking part in the debate in the House of Lords on December 8, spoke as follows regarding restrictions:
First of all, their own powers are circumscribed and restricted under their own constitutions granted by this country, under the operation of the Colonial Laws Validity Act, 1805, and under the well-known principle, which is not only true in theory but has been acted upon frequently, that as regards matters essentially affecting the mother country the British parliament at Westminster has a supreme authority over all dominions and colonial possessions.
Further on he said:
No one can say that the dominions, for instance, are in no way subordinate to the British parliament in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs. They are subordinate, not only in theory but in practice, in constitutional practice, in many directions both as regards their domestic and their external affairs.
And a little further on he added:
It has been authoritatively laid down that the obvious purpose and meaning of the Colonial Laws Validity Act are to reserve the

right of the imperial legislature to legislate for the colonies to which a local legislature has been given, and to make it impossible for the colonial legislatures to enact anything repugnant to the imperial legislature, but not otherwise to derogate from its general legislative authority. As a matter of fact, under the Colonial Law's Validity Act and what is known as the principle of reservation, a series of matters has been reserved or kept under the jurisdiction of the British parliament at Westminster. For this reason: although you may lay down a principle of this kind in very wide language, yet when you come to its operation you will find that in a considerable number of cases what may appear to be a mere act of a local legislature of a dominion is of a character that may substantially-I use that word purposely because it is a word that has been applied in legal language-affect the interests of the mother country.
Mr. -CAHAN:	That was Lord Parmoor.
The right hon. gentleman said he was quoting Lord Balfour.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: No, Lord Parmoor is putting forward the views that my hon. friend would wish to put forward.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Possibly I can present my
own views.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Exactly. Then may I read what Lord Balfour said in reply? What I have just read is the argument presented from the point of view-

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Of the agitator.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: He was president of the council in the Ramsay MacDonald government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
The answer
made by Lord Balfour is this:
I must honestly say that to this part of the speech I have the most fundamental objection. He seems to me to have approached the subject entirely in the wrong spirit. He does not deny that he sympathizes with those declarations; he does not deny that that is the sort of idea that he himself cherishes; but he says: "What folly to lay down the general principles on which this empire is now constructed. I think you should first settle all the preliminary details, and smooth away all the technical difficulties which have their origin in the long history of our overseas dominions."
I cannot imagine any policy from which I more profoundly differ. You are to set yourself every kind of problem, every sort of difficulty which may conceivably arise in the course of applying the broad principles of equality of status before you dare to announce that equality of status exists.
Can anything be more legal or less statesmanlike? I cannot even put myself in the

Imperial Conference-Mr. Mackenzie King
frame of mind of the noble Lord on that subject. He asks, for instance, if the Dominions want to separate from us what exactly would happen then, what sort of notice" ought to be given, by what procedure would it be done? You might as well consider all the causes of divorce before you decide upon the problems of matrimony.
Does not the noble Lord see that it would be impracticable for the conference of the Dominions and the Mother Country to meet at Westminster to say: "Well, on the whole we are inclined to think the idea of empire is one to which we may all look forward and which will embody equality of status, but just think of how many questions we must decide before we get to that point. Here is this difficulty and there is another difficulty arising out of the act of 1865. There are all these problems with regard to the Merchant Shipping Act. We must settle all those before we decide on what principle this collection of self-governing states is to work together." I boldly say to your Lordships' House that that is from beginning to end the wrong way of going to work. We have gone on exactly the opposite way.
Then, referring to a speech he himself had made before, Lord Balfour continued:
I said in reference to the relations between the mother country and the dominions:
"My own personal view' is that the relations are those necessarily of equality. None of us conceive that of this conglomeration of free states one is above the other. One may have more responsibility than another, one may be in more dangers than another, one may be closer to the centre of international complications than another, but all are on an equality. That is the very essence, as I understand it, of the British Empire. As to exactly what that equality involves, as to exactly w'hat degree of responsibility each has for the other, on that I personally think very little is gained by refining, discussing or defining."
Then he concludes:
Remember exactly what the position is. In this country we are all familiar v'itk the idea of equality between the self-governing portions of the empire. I will not give the quotations, but it has been stated by various high authorities for the last quarter of a century and has never, I think, been formally contradicted within these shores. But that is not the position in all the Dominions. In many of the Dominions there is a minority-in most cases, I dare say, a very small minority-u'ho are alw-ays following the train of thought which recommends itself so much to the noble Lord. They are always looking at these survivals of an earlier past and saying: "how can you consider that we in this or that Dominion are on an equality with the mother country w'hen we find still unrepealed this or that statute? If you are to allow that kind of statement to go uncontradicted, unqualified by the broad considerations of equality w'ith v'liich you ought to begin, of course you can get in an audience mixed up in local controversy a certain amount of opinion in favour of the assertion that, whatever talk may go on in England, in this or that Dominion things are far otherwise and the boasted equality between the various selfgoverning parts of our empire does not, in fact, exist. It does, in fact, exist.
What is contrary to the fact are these survivals of a previous condition of things, survivals which have no practical effect, W'hich have no practical interference with that equality w'hich each part of the self-governing parts of the empire may justly claim for itself, but which no doubt can be set out in a formal document which, if you choose to treat the w'hole thing as purely a question of law, might have an effect, and as I believe has had an effect, in local controversies overseas. There is but one way of getting rid of that difficulty, and getting rid of it forever, and that is to take advantage of the presence within our shores of the Prime Ministers, who are representative each of his own Dominion, meeting round a table discussing this question in all its aspects and coming unanimously to the conclusion which I have ventured to say represents British opinion, and to agree that it may be desirable to consider this or that difficulty in the future, but that the broad principle-never interfered with on any important point-stands, that no control is exercised by any single one of the self-governing parts of the empire over any other part of the empire.
That is as conclusive a statement of the position that the conference sought to lay down as it would be possible to present.
When my hon. friend at this moment asserts that it is all nonsense to talk about equality of status he runs completely counter to his hon. leader, who made a statement in this House in the course of the speech on the Address. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) outlined what had taken place at the different imperial conferences that have been held. He declared that the idea of equality of status was not a new one and that for many years past we had been claiming that equality. But he made one statement which was very emphatic and positive as to the time at which that equality had been recognized. Let me read to the House what the hon. member said. He is reported in Hansard at page 27, December 13, 1926, as follows:
The next conference was that of 1921. There had been a good deal of change in the position of the overseas dominions since the 1917 conference; not only had we been recognized as free and equal nations, but we had actually signed the treaty of Peace, I suppose the most memorable treaty of modern or of ancient times. There we stood in Paris shoulder to shoulder with the other nations of the W'orld and recognized as being on an equality w'ith Great Britain and the other nations.
Could there be a more positive statement than that or one more comprehensive? That is what the leader of the opposition said, and I wonder whether my hon. friend will differ from him. If he does, then there is considerable difference in the ranks of hon. gentlemen opposite. The hon. member went on to say:
1660	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Mackenzie King
Therefore when the conference met in London in 1921 a question immediately arose as to whether it was now necessary to call a constitutional conference pursuant to the resolution of 1917. The constitutional situation had greatly changed; our position had become definite and accepted.
That is the view of the leader of the opposition. Let me again point out that the question of equality of status is not a matter that has been determined by this last conference; it is one of political evolution. What this last conference has done has been to give to the world an authoritative statement of an agreement on the part of all parts of the empire to that broad principle of equality of status.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: How was that agreement evidenced?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: By a report unanimously adopted 'by the conference, which report was approved by the British government as well as by the representatives of other governments present.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Does approval of the Prime Minister constitute approval on the part of Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: I am afraid we shall have to wait forever before my hon. friend will approve it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: That is not a fair answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: If there is to be any approval at any time I doubt whether a more authoritative one could be found than that which the last Imperial conference gave.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Which the Prime Minister
of this country gave on behalf of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Which I agreed to, yes, on behalf of Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Could no more authoritative approval be given by Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: If my hon. friend thinks that in giving that approval I went contrary to the views of this parliament, I ask him to move a resolution to that effect and let us debate it in this House. If he does we shall get an expression of opinion on the part of parliament, and I venture to say that parliament will endorse the position taken by the Imperial conference on the question of equality of status.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: There are other things.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
It has taken a long time to secure this authoritative statement regarding the relationship between the dominions and the mother country. May 1
[Mr. Mackenzie King.J
remind the House that the first person to declare, in a manner which served to attract general attention that Canada was a nation, with an equality of status with other parts of the empire, owing a common allegiance to the king, was the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. This was at the time of Queen Victoria's diamond jubilee in 1S97. In that year, speaking on July 7 at the Constitutional Club, as reported in The Times on the following day, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
The British Empire is a galaxy of free nations. The bond of the British Empire is allegiance to the king, without distinction of race or colour.
I ask my hon. friend to compare that declaration made in 1897 with the declaration of the Imperial conference of 1927 and he will find that both essentials are identical. Each lays emphasis on the national character of the Dominions, each lays emphasis on the common bond of allegiance to the Sovereign. Sir -Wilfrid Laurier was decried by the friends of my hon. friend as being a separatist because he sought to give this country the status of a nation and equality in status with other parts of the British Empire, but the position Sir Wilfrid Laurier took at that time has at last not only been vindicated but come to be recognized throughout the British empire and throughout the world.
I would be very wide of the mark if I omitted as the most important of all the factors which have hastened this recognition the great part taken by this country and by the dominions as a whole throughout the period of the great war. The declaration we have here is virtually the declaration of the position of our Dominion as it would be expressed by the men who fought in the war, and who, through the general who led them at the close, gave expression to their views in the heart of London. I have in my hand a copy of an address which I had the privilege of listening to in London in 1919, delivered by Sir Arthur Ourrie who was, if I recollect aright, receiving the freedom of the city of London. The hon. member for Argenteui! (Sir George Perley) was at the time Canadian High Commissioner 'in London, and through his courtesy I had the privilege of going with him to the Mansion House and listening to this address. I desire to read a part of it to the House, because it seems to me to express exactly what the Imperial conference has expressed with respect to the status and position which should be recognized throughout the empire as existing between its different parts. On May 27, 1919, at the Mansion House, Sir Arthur Currie spoke as follows:

Imperial Conference-Mr. Guthrie
At this time and in this place all we can say now is that the war has brought about many rapid and drastic changes in the viewpoint of the dominions concerning their relations with the Motherland. They now believe that it is urgent that a new basis shall be found which will strengthen the British system and which will recognize that certain component parts of the empire have earned for themselves the status of nations, and they are anxious, among other things, that every suggestion of political inferiority shall be removed. In the many branches of war activities, either in the field or at home, as soldiers or as manufacturers, or in the sweeter realm of mercy, the dominions have proved themselves second to none, and have earned for themselves a proud place amongst the civilized nations of the world alongside Great Britain.
The national spirit of the dominions has been matured by the war, but the ties which bind the empire together have in no way been weakened. On the contrary, I believe there is now a strong feeling that machinery should be erected that would make out of the British Empire a constellation of nations free, equal, united by good will, common ideals, reciprocal confidence, all under one flag and one King. These nations, although enjoying absolute freedom in the working of their particular destinies, should have a voice commensurate with their_ singular interests in the empire as a whole. Under equal rights, equal privileges, they should, through the medium of the machinery provided, share equal duties one toward the other in the broadest spirit of cooperation, and in the councils of the world should speak definitely under the authority accruing to the combination of power, broad wisdom, and high ideals which it would represent. There is no reason why Canada, Australia, South Africa, and New Zealand, should not be to England in relation to the empire what Glasgow, Liverpool and Manchester are to London in relation to the United Kingdom, and I believe that a political system that would bring about the realization of this ideal would prove an everlasting benefit, not only to the empire s constituent parts, but to the world at large.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that this statement by Sir Arthur Currie, voicing as I believe it does the views of the men who fought overseas in the Great war, constitutes a statement of the position which exists at the present time throughout the empire, a position of equality of status between Great Britain and the selfgoverning dominions, and I believe it is a position which instead of challenging in any particular we should be proud to assert on every possible occasion.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the
House has been very glad to hear the exhaustive statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in regard to the proceedings of the Imperial conference held in London during October and November, 1926, which for the first time have been up for discussion in the parliament of Canada as a definite question. In introducing the subject this afternoon the right hon. Prime Minister stated that by agreement it was arranged that the discussion should come up in this way. By that language the Prime Minister could only have meant that by agreement this afternoon was fixed as the time for the discussion, because I never for one moment considered that a question of this kind would be brought up on a motion made by the government itself that you, Mr. Speaker, do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of supply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Let me say
to my hon. friend at once, that I meant we would take it up at this time; it was a matter of arrangement.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
An arrangement of time
but not method.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
I agree that the time was arranged but not the method, and when the suggestion was made to me there was nothing further from my mind than that such a method should be selected for this important discussion.
This matter was discussed to some extent at an earlier date this session, Mr. Speaker. On December 13 last', when the House was occupied in discussing the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the subject received some considerable attention, and reference was made this afternoon by the right hon. the Prime Minister to that debate. No objection was taken to his so doing and I presume the same courtesy will be accorded me, because it is my desire to make reference to the remarks of my right hon. friend on that occasion to show the idea I had with regard to the method to be adopted by the government in bringing this question to the attention of parliament. During the discussion in December last my right hon. friend made it abundantly clear that the report of the conference would be submitted to parliament in due course; he did so in precise and emphatic language which will be found at page 43 of Hansard:	.
It was a conference of representatives of the different governments, and everything that conference did, before it begins to bind a single part of the empire, is subject to the approval of not only the governments but also the parliaments of the different parts of the empire.
A little further down on the same page he used these words:
I may say to my hon. friend that the government intends to put the report before this House just as it appears, and to recommend its adoption.
1062	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Guthrie
There can. be little surprise, therefore, that I was misled by the positive statements made by the Prime Minister on December 13 last. I assumed that my right hon. friend would bring this report forward to-day in the form of a motion expressing the approval of this House of the report and the proceedings of the conference of 1926. When he spoke in this chamber on the 13th of December last he declared that he would do so: he meant to bring the report here and ask this House to confirm and approve it. But in the interval he has changed his mind for some mysterious reason best known to himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
May I give
my hon. friend the reason?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Not just now. I do not
want to be interrupted and I do not want to be discourteous either; but I myself do not interrupt and I do not like to be interrupted. For some mysterious reason best known to himself, which he did not give the House to-day, the Prime Minister has changed his method of procedure. He does not now ask parliament to approve this report. As I listened with the greatest respect and with the greatest attention to his remarks this afternoon I gathered that in his view all the consent, or assent, or approval, which this parliament need give had already been given by the Prime Minister when he supported the motion in the Imperial conference which carried the report. I must dissent entirely from that position. I submit to my right hon. friend and to the Minister of Justice that they never were authorized by this country or this parliament to go to the conference for any other purpose than to confer, to advise, and to consult, and the Prime Minister had not the power, nor had his Minister of Justice, nor had either or both of them, to commit this parliament or this country to a single proposal, and it cannot be done to-day save through the action of this House. It has always been laid down in this House, and I think in the conferee re itself, that all proceedings at these conferences are purely advisory.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
And my hon. friend the
Minister of Justice interjects the remark "hear, hear".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: It is a truism surely.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Does he agree with me
in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Surely.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Does he agree that this
parliament has not in any way, shape or form been committed upon the report of the conference?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Surely.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Then why the discussion this afternoon? Why take up the time of parliament further if approval of parliament is not asked by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and will not be asked by the Minister of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: It was not taken up in the British parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
I am not discussing the
action of the British parliament. I am talking of the action of this government, and of the statement made by the Prime Minister in this House on the 13th December last that this matter would be brought up, a report laid before parliament, and the approval of parliament sought. That has not been done. It should have been done; and I entirely dissent from the proposal that we in this country or in this parliament can be committed in any degree whatever by the action of the Prime Minister and his cabinet in a matter of this kind. I mention this particularly now in view of what took place at the conference of 1923. The danger of the situation is that unless we do take some definite action in regard to these proposals, as time goes on we may be taken to have acquiesced in them whether we have done so or not. That is precisely the difficulty in which we find ourselves in regard to the conference of 1923. In the conference of 1923 certain recommendations were made in regard to the negotiation and the ratification of treaties and carried unanimously. That conference was attended by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and by the then Minister of Justice, Sir Lomer Gouin. They heard the resolution in regard to treaties read and discussed at the conference; they both voted for it, at least they did not dissent, because the report says it was carried unanimously; but it has never been laid before this House for approval or adoption. What are the words of the resolution itself? It says:
The conference recommends for the acceptance of the governments of the empire represented, that the following procedure should be observed in the negotiation, signature and ratification of international agreements.
It recommends "for the acceptance of the governments concerned." Parliament has never approved that resolution. Is it possible that the government has approved it? Because "government" is the word used in the

Imperial Conference-Mr. Guthrie
resolution. Is it possible that an order in council has been passed by this government, of which parliament knows nothing, approving the resolution in respect of treaties passed in 1923? I do not think that any order in council has been passed. I do not think the government has ever approved the resolution of 1923. I am sure the House has never approved it. Now the difficulty is this: We have acted upon that resolution without approval. It may be said we have adopted it, and I think we should be very careful that we are not involved in the same manner in the present instance. In the year 1924, and again I think in the year 1925, treaties have been ratified and signed in accordance with that resolution passed at the conference of 1923, which was not to come into force until it was accepted by the governments of the selfgoverning dominions. This government has never accepted it so far as I know, but we have acted upon it and consequently we will be held to have ratified it.
Now I think my right hon. friend realizes that if we simply discuss the present resolution, if parliament takes no action upon it, if we allow it to lie upon the table without dissenting, we will be held, as the years go on, to have acquiesced in it and to be bound by it. I propose then to offer formal dissent, to make clear that this parliament has not approved of it and is not bound by it. I submit that the principle that ministers are entitled to go to these conferences and in any way commit this country is absolutely untenable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
No man could have made it plainer than the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier did in the conference of 1902, again in 1907, and again in 1911, when he even objected to the change of the name from "Imperial conference" to "Imperial council." He said the words "Imperial council" might imply a body which has some power to enact or to legislate. He dissented from that idea altogether, and made his dissent very marked and very plain. No one has ever considered, from his day down to the present time, that the mere reports of these conferences, although unanimously passed, committed anybody until they had been expressly approved by parliament.
My right hon. friend has brought this matter up in such a way that it is difficult to express ourselves without being charged with partisanship in so doing. No one knows better than my right hon. friend that any motion we may make, by way of amendment to the motion now before the chair, is a motion of want of confidence in this government; and nobody knows better than my right hon. friend that he can successfully stifle free discussion and the expression of free opinion on this question by simply saying to his followers behind him, "This is a want of confidence amendment and must be voted down." He has taken a strangely inappropriate opportunity to consider this question in an absolutely unpartisan manner.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend wishes to bring in a motion, I will undertake to say on behalf of the government that we shall not regard it as a want of confidence motion?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Whether he so regards it or not, it is, and it would be an amendment to a motion to go into supply. I think, however, my right'right hon. friend in his speech in the House to-day has discussed this question upon fairly broad principles and has so far as he possibly could, avoided that taint of partisanship which he is always inclined to impute to this side of the House in our discussions and as he did impute to me when I discussed this matter in December last. I will discuss this question upon just as high a plane and upon a plane just as nonpartisan as has my right hon. friend, and in the remarks which I propose to offer upon this matter I shall have no regard whatever to party politics. I shall have regard only for the well-being, present and future, as I see it, of the Dominion of Canada. It may be that many will be in absolute disagreement with the propositions which I propose to lay before this chamber before I conclude my remarks; but I am convinced that I am right in the view which I hold, and I discern in this proposal elements of the gravest danger to this country, although not perhaps in the immediate future. I do not say that serious dangers exists to-day; but what I fear in this report is that it opens the door to future possibilities which may end in serious consequences to this country and the time to avoid and to check the possibilities of future trouble is now.
The difficulty could have been avoided very easily by the insertion of a few words in this report. Had the Prime Minister and his colleague the Minister of Justice fully appreciated the whole matter involved in this report, a slight limitation or reservation in respect of Canada might have saved the situation. I do not for one moment say that the whole report is open to objection, far from it. In regard to most of it, I heartily agree with the Prime Minister. I could go over many of the statements which he has made to the House this afternoon, and in

Imperial Conjerence-Mr. Guthrie
regard to them I would have to express my full accord. Nor do I take issue with his remarks in regard to equality of status; I agree with him on that point. To my mind he laboured the question of equal status far too much in his speech this afternoon. We have always asserted an equality of status for this country; whether our assertion has at all times been well founded or not is another question. We have at all times during iny public life proclaimed it; we rejoice in it and we desire to maintain it. But any proposal which by any possibility may interfere in the future with the special conditions and circumstances which exist between peoples and provinces in this country we must avoid.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the six o'clock adjournment, while discussing the report of the Imperial conference of 1923, I had stated that that report had never been adopted by this House. I must express my thanks to my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) for having drawn to my attention that during the closing days of the last session of parliament a resolution was submitted to this House, which was adopted, approving of the resolution of the conference of 1923. I had looked through the records for 1924 and 1925, but I had not looked through those for the year 1926. I find, however, that during the last week of the last session the report of the conference of 1923 was formally adopted by a resolution of this House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend? I think he is mistaken. What was adopted was that particular part of the report which related to the signature, negotiation and ratification of treaties, but the report itself as a whole was not submitted to parliament.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: It is the resolution I was discussing this afternoon, which was made subject to the ratification of the governments of the various dominions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: That one resolution.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OP PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
My point was that it had never -been adopted, although we had acted upon it in regard to one or two treaties. For same reason or other, at the close of last session it was thought necessary to bring in a resolution to adopt that particular resolution of the Imperial conference of 1923. If it was

necessary to do so on that occasion, is it not far more necessary on the present occasion that a similar course should be taken by this House to adopt the much more important report which is now before us for consideration? Why, Sir, as I read the reports of the former Imperial conferences they fade into insignificance in contrast with the report of the last conference. The former reports deal with matters of minor interest as compared with the pronouncements made by the conference of 1926. In none of the former reports was there any recommendation which one might consider a recommendation for any constitutional change. But in this instance by the language of the report itself constitutional principles are discussed and recommendations are made involving what one must pronounce to be grave constitutional changes in this country.
Mr. Speaker, if ever there was a time when definite action should be taken by parliament in regard to an Imperial conference report that time is now. Indeed, so various have been the statements made and the opinions expressed in regard to this report by ministers who actually took part in the conference as representatives of this country and by others who represented other parts of the British Empire, so various and so diversified have been the expressions of opinion in regard to what the conference actually did, that the public of this country has no clear idea of what actually took place from wdiat has been actually reported. I place side by side the statements made by three of the prime ministers who attended the conference of 1926. First, I take the statement made by the Prime Minister of Australia when he was in Canada in January last as reported in the press at the time. He said:
There is nothing really new in the status or relations of the British dominions as a result of the recent conference. The rights now enjoyed have existed ever since the termination of the war.
